lesson.title: From Grams to Grams: Mass-to-Mass Stoichiometry
lesson.summary: Mass-to-mass calculations bookend the mole ratio method with a molar mass conversion on each side, letting you go directly from grams of one substance to grams of another in a reaction.
lesson.body:
Stoichiometry laid out the general roadmap, and Molar Mass gave you the conversion factor, grams per mole, that connects a measurable mass to a countable number of moles. Mole-to-Mole Ratios covered the middle step of that roadmap, converting moles of one substance into moles of another using the coefficients of a balanced equation. Mass-to-mass calculations put all three pieces together, since balanced equations relate moles directly, but laboratory measurements are almost always made in grams, not moles.

The roadmap has three steps. First, convert the given mass of substance A into moles of A, by dividing by the molar mass of A. Second, convert moles of A into moles of substance B, using the mole ratio built from the coefficients of the balanced equation. Third, convert moles of B into a mass of B, by multiplying by the molar mass of B.

Return once more to propane combustion: C3H8(g) + 5 O2(g) -> 3 CO2(g) + 4 H2O(g). How many grams of CO2 form when 88.2 g of C3H8 burns completely in excess oxygen? Step one: the molar mass of C3H8 is about 44.1 g/mol, 3 carbons at 12.01 g/mol plus 8 hydrogens at 1.01 g/mol. Moles of C3H8 equal 88.2 g divided by 44.1 g/mol, which equals 2.00 mol. Step two: the mole ratio of CO2 to C3H8 from the balanced equation is 3 to 1, so moles of CO2 equal 2.00 mol times 3, which equals 6.00 mol. Step three: the molar mass of CO2 is about 44.0 g/mol, 1 carbon at 12.01 g/mol plus 2 oxygens at 16.00 g/mol each. Mass of CO2 equals 6.00 mol times 44.0 g/mol, which equals 264 g.

A common mistake is trying to skip straight from grams of A to grams of B using the mole ratio as if it applied to masses directly. It does not, because the coefficients in a balanced equation count particles, meaning moles, not grams, and different substances have different molar masses. In this example, 88.2 g of C3H8 produced 264 g of CO2, roughly three times the starting mass, which makes sense once you notice that each mole of C3H8 produces 3 moles of a product with a molar mass close to its own. Skipping the mole conversions and multiplying grams by the coefficient ratio directly would have given a wrong answer that only accidentally resembles a real calculation.
